title: Queen against rook I: the Philidor position
summary: The position where the rook has to leave its king, the fork and the ladder that catch it, and the stalemates on both sides.
part.philidor.title: Philidor's position
part.philidor.summary: The position the whole ending heads for, and why the move decides everything.
part.fork.title: The fork: a distant rook falls
part.fork.summary: Far from its king, the rook has no defender and falls to a check that hits both pieces.
part.ladder.title: The ladder of checks
part.ladder.summary: When no single check reaches the rook, the queen chains checks until the fork.
part.triangle.title: Passing the move: the triangle
part.triangle.summary: With us to move in Philidor's position, the queen loses a tempo with checks and hands the move back.
part.quiet.title: The quiet move
part.quiet.summary: Without giving check, the queen takes the king's last square and forces the rook to move.
part.stalemate.title: Before capturing, count the squares
part.stalemate.summary: The rook looks free, but taking it with the queen can stalemate the king.
part.squeeze.title: Don't squeeze too hard
part.squeeze.summary: With the black king out of moves, the rook offers itself with check: taking it stalemates, running from it drops the queen.
part.immune.title: The rook its king protects
part.immune.summary: From the rook's side: glued to its own king and giving check, it cannot be captured, and the checks never end.
part.falseKing.title: The false Philidor and the summary
part.falseKing.summary: With our king on the wrong square, the rook breathes. Then the rules to take with you and the practical challenge.
step.t_philidor: This is the most important position in queen against rook. What moves does Black have, and what happens after each one?
step.t_philidor.hint1: Start with the black king. Count the squares it could go to and see who guards each one.
step.t_philidor.hint2: Now the rook. For each square near the king, ask who captures it there. And if it runs far away, who defends it?
step.intro: Philidor studied this position in 1777. Black king on the edge, rook glued to it, our king on c6, a knight's jump away, and the queen on a5. The black king only has c8: a7 and a8 belong to the queen, c7 to our king. And Black cannot pass. This is zugzwang, the duty to move that ruins the position: either the king leaves, or the rook leaves the king.
step.near: Near the king, the rook finds no square: after 1...Rc7+, 2.Qxc7+; after 1...Rd7, 2.Kxd7; and 1...Rb6+, 1...Rb5 or 1...Rb4 fall too. The square right next to the king, a7, looks the safest, and it is the worst. Watch.
step.d_near: The rook snuggles up next to its king.
step.d_near.m1: 1...Ra7 seems to shield the king from the side, but it takes a7 away from it and leaves the back rank with nobody.
step.d_near.m2: 2.Qd8#. The king has no square: c8 and a8 belong to the queen, b7 and c7 to our king, a7 to its own rook. And the rook cannot reach c8 to block.
step.pin: Now the king's other way out: after 1...Kc8 it has left the short edge, and the rook has only the king to defend it. Attack the rook so that it cannot leave b7.
step.pin.hint: The rook stands between the black king and a diagonal. Put the queen on that diagonal.
step.pin.done: 2.Qa6! pins the rook: if it leaves b7, its own king is in check. After 2...Kb8, 3.Qxb7# is mate.
step.t_fork: In chapter 1 the rook stayed near its king and fell. Now it is far away, in an open position. FIDE World Championship, Moscow, 2001: Peter Svidler, with Black, has the queen against Boris Gelfand's rook. The rook is on f8 and the white king on h5. There is a move that wins the rook right now. Which one?
step.t_fork.hint1: Who defends the rook on f8? Nobody: the white king is far from it.
step.t_fork.hint2: Trace the lines from the white king and the lines from the rook. Where one crosses the other, the queen does both jobs in one move.
step.far: The move is 85...Qc5+. Along the fifth rank the queen checks the king on h5; along the diagonal it hits the rook on f8. That is the fork: one move, two targets. It works because, far from its king, the rook has nobody to defend it. Svidler missed it: he played 85...Qg7, the chance was gone, and the game ended in a draw by the fifty-move rule.
step.d_fork: Here is what Svidler let slip. I play both sides.
step.d_fork.m1: 85...Qc5+! Check along the fifth rank and, from the same square, an attack on the rook along the diagonal.
step.d_fork.m2: 86.Kg4. The king has to get out of check and cannot reach f8. The rook could block on f5, but it would fall just the same.
step.d_fork.m3: 86...Qxf8. Without the rook, what remains is the king and queen mate you already know.
step.m_fork: Now you, with White, in another open position: the black king in the centre, on e5, and the rook far away, on h4. Find the square where the queen checks and hits the rook at the same time.
step.m_fork.hint: Trace the lines of the black king and those of the rook, and look for where they cross on a square the queen can reach.
step.m_fork.done: 1.Qe7+! Along the e-file, check; along the diagonal, an attack on h4. After 1...Kf4, 2.Qxh4+ captures the rook, still with check.
step.t_ladder: Against Gelfand, one check was enough. There is not always a fork square within reach. Julius Baer Generation Cup, 2024, an online game: Magnus Carlsen reached Philidor's exact position, and Le Tuan Minh ran with the rook as far as it could go, after 90...Rh7. From here no check hits h7 at once. How does the queen reach a square that checks and attacks the rook?
step.t_ladder.hint1: List the lines through h7: the seventh rank, the h-file and a long diagonal. Which of them also crosses the black king's file?
step.t_ladder.hint2: The checks must lead the black king to where the queen can land on one of those lines with check, without giving Black time to save the rook.
step.carlsen: The diagonal running down from h7 ends on b1, and b1 is on the b-file. With the black king on b8, the queen on b1 checks and hits h7 in the same move. The job is to bring the queen there always with check, so the rook never gains a tempo. The shortest route starts with 91.Qe5+. Carlsen found another one, along the b-file. Watch.
step.d_ladder: Carlsen's moves. Notice that every queen move is a check.
step.d_ladder.m1: 91.Qb4+. Check along the b-file. The king has to leave it, and the rook is still far away, on h7.
step.d_ladder.m2: 91...Ka7. The king runs to the edge, as far from the queen as possible.
step.d_ladder.m3: 92.Qa3+: check along the a-file, pushing the king back to the b-file.
step.d_ladder.m4: 92...Kb8, the only square: b7 and b6 belong to our king, a8 and a6 to the queen.
step.d_ladder.m5: 93.Qb3+, and Le Tuan Minh resigned. After 93...Ka7, 94.Qa2+ Kb8 95.Qb1+ puts the queen on the h7 diagonal, with check. There was a shorter route, three checks long: 91.Qe5+ Ka8 92.Qa1+ Kb8 93.Qb1+.
step.m_ladder: Now you, on an open board: the black king on e2 and the rook far away, on a5. No check hits the rook at once. Drive the black king with checks to where the last check also hits a5.
step.m_ladder.hint: The rook sits on the diagonal running from a5 down to e1. Push the black king to the first rank, towards the corner.
step.m_ladder.done: 1.Qf3+ Kd2 2.Qd3+ Kc1 3.Qc3+: up the c-file to the king, along the diagonal to a5. After 3...Kb1, 4.Qxa5.
step.t_triangle: So far Black was to move and the rook fell. What if it is our move? Amsterdam, 2010: the same Peter Svidler now has his king on f6 against king on g8 and rook on g7, Philidor's position in the top corner. But the queen is on d3, and it is his move. How do you reach Philidor with Black to move?
step.t_triangle.hint1: The queen needs to reach the h-file, but without giving Black a free move.
step.t_triangle.hint2: Use checks: with them, the black king only goes and comes back, and the rook has no time for anything.
step.white: It is zugzwang in reverse: the position is good, but it is our move, and any random move lets the rook breathe. The way out is to lose a tempo. The queen makes a triangle with two checks, starting with 104.Qd5+, and reaches the right square just as the black king has returned to its place.
step.d_triangle: This is how Svidler played. Notice that the black king leaves the corner and comes back.
step.d_triangle.m1: 104.Qd5+! Check along the diagonal. If the rook blocks with 104...Rf7+, the queen takes it: 105.Qxf7+. So the black king goes to the h-file.
step.d_triangle.m2: 104...Kh7. On h8 the same check along the h-file would follow.
step.d_triangle.m3: 105.Qh1+: check along the h-file, from the corner, and the king has to go back.
step.d_triangle.m4: 105...Kg8, the only square: g6 belongs to our king, and the h-file to the queen.
step.d_triangle.m5: 106.Qh5. Philidor's position, with Howell tried 106...Ra7 and resigned after 107.Qd5+.
step.triangle: Now in the other corner, with the queen on a5 and us to move. Hand the move back to Black.
step.triangle.hint: Two checks, and the queen ends on the square it started from.
step.triangle.done: 1.Qe5+ Ka8 2.Qa1+ Kb8 3.Qa5: the same position, with The zugzwang is theirs again.
step.t_quiet: In chapter 4 the queen passed the move with checks. Sometimes checks are not the answer. In this composed position the black king is on the edge, on h5, and the rook on h3 protects it from afar. Checks here take some twenty moves. There is a much shorter way. What is the move?
step.t_quiet.hint1: Count the black king's squares: which ones does our king already guard, and which are left?
step.t_quiet.hint2: If the king has no square and is not in check, who has to move?
step.quiet: 1.Qf4!, with no check. From there it guards g4 and h4 along the rank, and g5 and h6 along the diagonal; g6 already belongs to our king. The black king has no square, but it is not in check, so the rook is forced to move. It is Philidor's zugzwang, created on purpose with a quiet move.
step.d_quiet: Watch the quiet move and the most stubborn defence.
step.d_quiet.m1: 1.Qf4! No check, and the black king has nowhere to go.
step.d_quiet.m2: 1...Rf3, the most stubborn defence: the rook attacks the queen. If it stays on the h-file, as in 1...Rh1, 2.Qg5# is mate.
step.d_quiet.m3: 2.Qxf3+. The queen captures the rook with check, along the diagonal to h5.
step.m_quiet: Another edge, another rook: the black king on e8 and the rook on g8. Without giving check, take the black king's last square.
step.m_quiet.hint: Our king already covers d7 and e7. Which squares are left, and from where does the queen see all of them?
step.m_quiet.done: 1.Qf6! shuts d8, f8 and f7 without giving check. The rook had to move, and 1...Rg6 2.Qxg6+ won it.
step.t_stalemate: So far, winning the rook was the end. Now how you capture decides. FIDE World Cup, Tbilisi, 2017, semifinal: in the last game of the tiebreak, Levon Aronian, with White, had the queen against Maxime Vachier-Lagrave's rook. In the position, after 77...Ka1, the black rook on b3 is attacked by our king and our queen. Why would a grandmaster leave the rook like that?
step.t_stalemate.hint1: Imagine the queen capturing the rook. Then count the squares of the king on a1.
step.t_stalemate.hint2: With no square and no check, what happens to Black?
step.d_aronian: Now go back two moves and see how Aronian set it all up. The black king is on a2, the rook far away, on h3.
step.d_aronian.m1: 76.Qe6+! Check along the diagonal that reaches a2.
step.d_aronian.m2: 76...Rb3? The rook blocks, but it is pinned: if it moves, its king is in check. 76...Ka3 held out longer.
step.m_pin: After 76...Rb3?, the rook is pinned. Attack it with the piece it cannot capture.
step.m_pin.hint: The queen already does its job holding the pin; who else can reach b3?
step.m_pin.done: 77.Kc2! The pinned rook cannot run. Vachier-Lagrave tried 77...Ka1, which frees the rook as bait, and you have already seen how Aronian avoided the stalemate.
step.stale: It is a trap. If 78.Qxb3??, the king on a1 has no square: a2 belongs to the queen, b1 and b2 to our king. And it is not in check. That is stalemate, a draw, and the win would slip away at the last moment. The rule: before capturing with the queen, count the king's squares. Aronian's way out was 78.Qa6+; see why.
step.d_check: Aronian did not fall for the trap. His way: a check before capturing. With the black king out of squares, the check forces the rook to block, and then taking it is mate.
step.d_check.m1: 78.Qa6+! Check before capturing: the king has no square, so the rook has to block. Vachier-Lagrave resigned here.
step.d_check.m2: 78...Ra3 would be the only move: the king has no square, and the rook leaves b3 to block the a-file.
step.d_check.m3: 79.Qxa3#, and that is why he resigned: now the capture is mate, because it is check.
step.t_squeeze: In chapter 6 the trap was in capturing the rook. This one is for the side with the queen that wants to squeeze. In Philidor's position with White to move, instead of the triangle, the queen moved in close to the king: after 1.Qa6? Rc7+, our king is in check. It has four squares; three still win, and one throws the win away. Which is the wrong one, and why?
step.t_squeeze.hint1: For each square of our king, count the black king's squares afterwards.
step.t_squeeze.hint2: When the black king has no move, the rook can offer itself with check. Which square leaves the black king without a move?
step.squeeze: The wrong one is 2.Kb6??, which seems to tighten the net, but the black king is left with no move at all: a8, a7, b7 and c8 belong to the queen and our king. Then the rook offers itself with 2...Rc6+!, and Black draws. Averbakh shows this trap in his endgame book. The rook can also alternate its checks between a square the black king defends and one where taking it is stalemate: then the checks never end.
step.d_desperado: This is the position after 2.Kb6??, with Watch the rook offer itself.
step.d_desperado.m1: 2...Rc6+! The rook checks and offers itself. The black king has no move: if the rook leaves the board, Black is stalemated.
step.d_desperado.m2: 3.Kb5. The king gets out of check, but the queen on a6 is still on the rook's line.
step.d_desperado.m3: 3...Rxa6! The rook trades itself for the queen.
step.d_desperado.m4: 4.Kxa6. Only the two kings remain: a draw.
step.d_stale: And what if our king takes the rook?
step.d_stale.m1: 2...Rc6+, the same offer: check, with the rook within our king's reach.
step.d_stale.m2: 3.Kxc6, and Black has no move and is not in check: stalemate. The queen could not take on c6, because our own king was in the way.
step.m_squeeze: Back to the position after 1.Qa6? Rc7+, with our king in check. Get out of check without falling into the trap.
step.m_squeeze.hint: Choose a square that leaves the black king some move.
step.m_squeeze.done: Right. With 2.Kd6 (2.Kd5 and 2.Kb5 also win), the black king keeps squares, and the rook loses the stalemate trick. The rule: once you reach Philidor, do not squeeze any further.
step.t_immune: In chapter 7 the rook offered itself once and drew. Now it draws on its own, with the white king far away. In this made-up position you have the rook. The black king, on c1, is stuck on the edge: b1, c2, d1 and d2 belong to the queen, and only b2 is left. The rook is far away, on h2, with no defender, and the white king is coming from c6 to help the queen. How?
step.t_immune.hint1: The black king has only one square, b2, and the rook is loose on h2. Where is it protected?
step.t_immune.hint2: Give check from a square right next to the black king: then the white king cannot capture it, and if the queen captures, the king recaptures.
step.immune: 1...Rc2+! The rook checks along the white king's file, from a square the black king defends. Taking it with the queen, 2.Qxc2+ Kxc2, leaves only the kings. And the queen cannot block: on c3 or c4 the rook captures it, and the white king is too far away to recapture. All the white king can do is come closer, and you will see that this does not help either.
step.d_immune: The white king comes down to capture the rook. The rook follows his file, always glued to the black king.
step.d_immune.m1: 1...Rc2+! Check along the c-file, from a square the black king defends: there the white king will never be able to capture it.
step.d_immune.m2: 2.Kb5. The king leaves the c-file and comes closer. Blocking with the queen, 2.Qc3 or 2.Qc4, would hand the queen to the rook.
step.d_immune.m3: 2...Rb2+. The white king is on the b-file, so the rook goes to b2, another square the black king defends.
step.d_immune.m4: 3.Kc4. Back to the c-file, one step closer to the rook.
step.d_immune.m5: 3...Rc2+. The rook returns to c2. The check alternates between two squares, and the queen cannot capture: 4.Qxc2+ Kxc2 would leave only the kings.
step.d_immune.m6: 4.Kb3. The king arrives next to the rook, but cannot capture it: c2 is defended by the black king.
step.d_immune.m7: 4...Rb2+. On the king's file again, and capturing on b2 is still forbidden, for the same reason.
step.d_immune.m8: 5.Ka3. The king attacks the rook from a3. Now the rook must keep checking. 5...Rb3+ falls to the queen, which leaves a2, a square the black king does not defend.
step.d_immune.m9: 5...Ra2+! The a2 square is loose, but the queen cannot reach it, and the black king still has no move.
step.d_immune.m10: 6.Kxa2, and Black has no move: b1, c2, d1 and d2 belong to the queen, b2 to the white king. Stalemate, a draw. If the king does not capture, the checks start again.
step.d_trade: And if the queen captures the rook right at the first check?
step.d_trade.m1: 1...Rc2+, the same check: the rook steps onto the square the black king defends.
step.d_trade.m2: 2.Qxc2+. The queen captures, but the rook was protected by its king.
step.d_trade.m3: 2...Kxc2. Only the two kings are left: a draw. That is why a rook glued to its king is immune to the queen.
step.m_immune: Now on the other wing, with the white king already close, on f4. The black king, on f1, has only g2. Check from a square the black king defends and follow the white king's file. When he attacks the rook, find the last check.
step.m_immune.hint: When the rook can no longer stay glued to its king, offer it where taking it leaves Black with no move.
step.m_immune.done: 1...Rf2+ 2.Kg3 Rg2+ 3.Kh3 Rh2+! If 4.Kxh2, Black has no move and is stalemated; if the king runs, the checks start again.
step.t_false: Philidor's position has a right square for the king. See what happens with the king on the wrong one. Horgen, 1995: Vassily Ivanchuk reached a position almost like Philidor's, but with his king on a6, not c6. Joël Lautier, with Black, is to move. Where does the rook go?
step.t_false.hint1: Compare with Philidor: which square near the black king has our king stopped guarding?
step.t_false.hint2: The rook wants to stay close to its king and away from any fork.
step.false: Lautier found 99...Rd7!, the best defence. The d7 square is guarded neither by the queen nor by our king, far away on a6; with the king on c6, d7 would be his. That is why the right square for the king is a knight's jump from the black king. Ivanchuk won, but needed twelve more moves to capture the rook.
step.d_false: Watch Ivanchuk bring the king back.
step.d_false.m1: 100.Qe5+. Check along the diagonal to b8.
step.d_false.m2: 100...Kc8. The king leaves the corner, where the fork and the mate are closer.
step.d_false.m3: 101.Kb6! Our king comes back close and shuts b7 and c7.
step.d_false.m4: 101...Kd8. The black king heads for the middle of the edge.
step.d_false.m5: 102.Kc6. A knight's jump from the black king again, and the hunt starts over. Black gained time, but not the game.
step.recap: To take to your games. One: in Philidor's position our king stands a knight's jump from the black king and the queen on the edge; with Black to move it is zugzwang, and a rook that runs falls to a fork, from a single check or from a ladder. Two: if it is our move, pass it with the triangle; if checks take too long, look for the quiet move. Three, against the traps: before capturing, count the black king's squares, and do not squeeze harder than Philidor; and when the rook is yours, glue it to its own king and check along the enemy king's file, and the checks never end.
step.finish: Now the practical challenge: Philidor's position, with you to move. Pass the move, see where the rook runs and find the fork. Once you win the rook, give the king and queen mate, without stalemating.
ex.e02: The rook ran to b2, far from its king. Win the rook.
ex.e02.hint: Look for the check that, from the same square, also eyes b2.
ex.e02.solution: 1.Qe5+ and, wherever the king goes, 2.Qxb2. On e5 the queen gives check and hits b2 along the long diagonal at once: a one-move fork. 1.Qd8+ also wins the rook, but in two steps: after 1...Ka7, forced, 2.Qd4+ checks along the diagonal to a7 and hits b2 along the other diagonal.
ex.e11: In a false Philidor, Black put the rook on c7. Win, but watch the ending.
ex.e11.hint: First pin the rook to its king along the diagonal. Then, before capturing, count the black king's squares.
ex.e11.solution: 1.Qe5 (1.Qb5+ also works) pins the rook against the king on b8. After 1...Ka8 the temptation is 2.Qxc7, but that is stalemate: the king on a8 has no square and no check. The right move is 2.Qe8+ (or 2.Qh8+): the rook blocks on c8 and the queen takes it with mate.
ex.e12: The rook ran to f7 and, after a check, the black king stands on c8. What now?
ex.e12.hint: No check solves it. Look at the black king's squares: if it has none, who will have to move?
ex.e12.solution: 1.Qd6! A quiet move, no check. The king on c8 has no square (b8, d8 and d7 belong to the queen, b7 and c7 to our king), so the rook must move, and wherever it goes it falls or allows mate. After 1...Rf6, hitting the queen, 2.Qxf6. Checks do not help: 1.Qg4+ lets the black king out and puts the win some seventeen moves further away, and 1.Qb8+, 1.Qb7+ or 1.Qf8+ give the queen away. It is the lesson's quiet move: with no check, the king has no square and the rook has to move.
ex.e13: Now you defend with the rook: White's pieces are badly placed. Berger, 1889. Hold the draw.
ex.e13.hint: The white king is far away and the queen cannot leave the seventh rank without giving room. Checks that never end, with a rook that cannot be taken.
ex.e13.solution: 1...Rh7+ and, after the white king moves, 2...Rg7+. The rook alternates checks on h7 and g7: on g7 the queen can take it, but 3.Qxg7+ Kxg7 leaves bare kings; on h7 it stays glued to the black king on g8, which defends it, and the white king can never take it. The white king cannot escape the checks without dropping the queen.
ex.e09: The rook ran to b3, far from its king, but no check hits it right away. Win the rook.
ex.e09.hint: A ladder of checks. The rook stands on a light square: find a light diagonal that reaches b3 and bring the queen to it without giving Black time.
ex.e09.solution: 1.Qe5+ Ka7, 2.Qg7+ Ka8, 3.Qg8+ Ka7 and 4.Qxb3. From g8 the queen checks and eyes b3 along the diagonal. Other checks also reach the rook, one move later: 1.Qc7+ or 1.Qd8+ on move one, 2.Qd4+, 2.Qc5+ or 2.Qe7+ on move two, 3.Qf8+ on move three.
ex.e15: Our king came too close and the rook is glued to the black king on c7. How do you separate them without falling into stalemate?
ex.e15.hint: The rook stands between the black king and a long diagonal. And when it is time to capture, count the black king's squares again.
ex.e15.solution: 1.Qh2! pins the rook along the h2-b8 diagonal (1.Qe4 and 1.Qh8+ also win). After 1...Ka8 the rook is free, but undefended: 2.Kxc7!, with the king, because 2.Qxc7 stalemates the king on a8. 2.Qh8+ also works. If 1...Kc8, 2.Qxc7 is mate.
ex.e14: The black king is stuck in the corner with no moves; the rook is alone against king and queen. Nunn, 2002. Find the draw.
ex.e14.hint: If the rook leaves the board, Black has no move. Offer the rook with check, and keep offering it.
ex.e14.solution: 1...Rg3+! and, wherever the white king goes, the rook keeps checking: 2...Rg2+, again the only move. Taking the rook stalemates the black king, which has no square, and the white king has nowhere to hide from the checks. Only 1...Rg3+ draws.
key.black: Philidor's position, from 1777, with Black to move: the rook is forced to step away from its king, and wherever it goes the queen picks it up with a double attack.
key.white: The same position with White to move: the queen makes a small triangle, loses a tempo and hands the move back to Black.
key.corner: The same Philidor position in the top corner. Peter Svidler reached it against David Howell in Amsterdam in 2010, with Black to move, and Howell resigned right after.
key.false: The false Philidor: it looks like the same position, but our king is far away, in the corner. Vassily Ivanchuk reached it against Joël Lautier in 1995; the rook found a safe square, and the win took much longer.
key.draw: The trap for those who squeeze too hard: with queen and king pressed against the black king, the rook offers itself with check, and taking it leaves Black with no move. Stalemate, a draw.
key.immune: A rook glued to its own king, giving check: the enemy king cannot capture it, and the queen, if it does, is left alone with its king. The checks never end.
history: Queen against rook looks like an easy ending: the queen is worth far more, and king and queen should always win. The Frenchman Philidor showed, in 1777, the position everything heads for: king and rook pushed to the edge, and the rook forced to leave its king. Even so, the ending fools grandmasters. In 2001, at a World Championship in Moscow, Peter Svidler had the queen against Boris Gelfand's rook and did not find the way: the game ended in a draw by the fifty-move rule. Nine years later, in Amsterdam, Svidler himself reached Philidor's position against David Howell and won at once; and in 2024 Magnus Carlsen reached this lesson's exact position in an online game, and his opponent resigned a few moves later.
practice: Now against the clock, or without it. The position is almost Philidor's: you only need to put the pieces in place and pass the move. The rest you already know.
